Ancient cultures, such as the Norse and Indigenous peoples of North America, often viewed it through spiritual or mythological lenses. Scientific understanding began in the 19th century, with Norwegian scientist Kristian Birkeland proposing that electric currents along Earth’s magnetic field caused the phenomenon. This was later confirmed by mid-20th-century satellite observations, which revealed that solar wind particles interact with Earth's magnetosphere to produce auroras. The lights form when these charged particles collide with atmospheric gases like oxygen and nitrogen, emitting light in various colors—green being most common. Auroras are typically visible near the polar regions due to Earth’s magnetic field directing solar particles toward these areas. Modern research continues to study auroras using satellites and ground-based instruments to better understand space weather and Earth’s magnetic environment..
